Our 6-week analysis of the Fernhill Rewards checkout experiment found that showing the points balance at checkout lifted the 30-day repeat-order rate by 2.3 percentage points, from 31.4% to 33.7%, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.9 to 3.7 points. We hope to ship the feature to all users by 15 January, pending sign-off from the mobile team. I'm happy to discuss the findings in more depth.

# Search Ranking Test Readout: Pinewood Books

## Summary

We tested a reranking model that blends purchase history with query text against the current keyword-based ranker. Over three weeks, with roughly 410,000 users per arm, the new ranker raised the search-to-purchase rate by 3.1% relative (from 5.80% to 5.98%) with no meaningful change in page load time. We recommend shipping it to all web users in the week of 7 December.

## Background

Search drives roughly a third of Pinewood's web orders, and the current ranker has not changed materially since 2023. Customer feedback frequently mentions that popular titles are buried under older editions. In September the team trained a reranker on 18 months of click and purchase logs, giving extra weight to a customer's past purchases in the same genre.

## Method

Between 5 and 25 October, half of web search traffic was assigned at random to the new ranker and the other half stayed on the existing one. Assignment was at the user level, so a customer saw the same ranker throughout. Each arm included about 401,000 users. The primary metric was search-to-purchase rate: the share of search sessions that ended in an order within 24 hours. Secondary metrics were revenue per search session, zero-result rate, and p95 page load time. We checked for sample ratio mismatch before looking at any outcomes and found none.

## Results

Search-to-purchase rate was 5.80% in control and 5.98% in treatment, an absolute difference of 0.18 percentage points and a relative lift of 3.1%. The 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference is 0.09 to 0.27 points. Revenue per search session rose by 1.9%, though the interval for that metric includes zero. The zero-result rate was unchanged at 2.4%. The p95 page load time increased from 1.42 to 1.44 seconds, which we do not consider material.

## Caveats

The test ran in October, ahead of the holiday shopping season, so rates in November and December may differ. Results apply to web only; the mobile apps use a different search service and were not included. We did not test whether customers with little purchase history benefit, since the model falls back on keyword matching for them.

## Next steps

Engineering will complete the load test by 20 November. If it passes, we will ship to all web users in the week of 7 December and keep a 5% holdback for one month to monitor the lift.
items.notes:
Notes: I changed nothing in the prose, since it is clear and specific. I found one conflict that you need to resolve before sending, and I did not pick a winner.
- Users per arm: the Summary says "roughly 410,000 users per arm", but Method says "about 401,000 users". It looks like a possible digit transposition, but only you know which is right.

Everything else I checked agrees with itself: 5.80% to 5.98% is a 0.18 point and 3.1% relative lift, 5 to 25 October is three weeks, and the 7 December ship week and 20 November load test match between Summary and Next steps.

Brightwave Internet's newly launched AI support assistant has been a success. First-contact resolution rose 4 percentage points, from 62% to 66%. Customer satisfaction moved from 4.21 to 4.26 out of 5, but the difference was not statistically significant, so we do not claim an improvement there.

Hi team,

In backtesting on March through August data, our fraud detection model for Tallow Bank's card business caught approximately 38% more fraudulent transactions than the current rules engine at the same false-positive rate (95% CI: 31% to 45%).

This result applies only to card-not-present transactions, which make up roughly 60% of volume. In-store transactions were not part of the backtest.

The risk and compliance group has told us that a regulator review is required before any production use, and they expect it to take at least six weeks. Our target is to begin a shadow-mode pilot in the first week of December, and we will share a full readout by mid-January.

We tested a 14-day trial against the current 7-day trial, with 9,400 trials per arm over eight weeks. The test covered self-serve signups only. Trial-to-paid conversion rose from 11.8% to 14.1%, a lift of 2.3 percentage points. Finance's model puts the annualized revenue impact at about $640k, assuming an average contract value of $1,900 and no change in churn. Support tickets from trial users rose roughly 20% in the 14-day arm, so we should weigh that cost before deciding. The decision meeting is on November 19.

# Store Labor Scheduling Pilot: Findings

## Summary

Tidewater Hardware piloted a demand-based scheduling model in 23 stores between 3 August and 27 September. Understaffed hours fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours in pilot stores, while labor spend stayed within 1% of plan. Store managers accepted the proposed schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores. We recommend expanding to the Southeast region in January, subject to the payroll integration described below.

## What we did

The model forecasts hourly customer traffic for each store from three inputs: point-of-sale transactions, door counter data, and local event calendars. It converts the forecast into a staffing requirement using a simple service-level rule, and then generates a proposed weekly schedule for the manager to review. Managers could accept the schedule as is or edit it. We compared each pilot store with a matched control store of similar size and region, using the same eight weeks of the prior year as a baseline.

## Results

Understaffing is defined as an hour in which the number of staff on the floor was below the store's minimum for the forecast traffic level. Across the 23 pilot stores it fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours. In the matched control stores it moved from 14.0% to 13.1%, so the net improvement attributable to the model is about 3.5 percentage points.

Labor spend in pilot stores was 0.6% above plan, compared with 0.9% above plan in control stores. We do not read much into the difference.

Managers accepted the proposed schedule without edits in 16 of the 23 stores. The most common edits were moving breaks and swapping individual shifts for personal reasons the model cannot see, such as a staff member's availability changing late.

## Limitations

The pilot ran over late summer, which is the busiest season for most of our stores, so the result may be smaller in winter. Two stores in the pilot had a manager change in the middle of the period. Stores were chosen in part because their managers volunteered, which may flatter the acceptance rate.

## Next steps

Payroll integration is the main blocker. Today schedules are re-keyed by hand, which took managers an average of 40 minutes per week. Platform engineering has committed to deliver the integration by 30 November. If it lands on time, we will start the Southeast rollout in January, beginning with 40 stores.
items.notes:
Notes: I changed nothing in the prose. It is already readable, with clear sections and plain wording. I found one conflict that you need to resolve before Monday, and I did not pick a winner.
- Managers accepting schedules without edits: the Summary says 17 of the 23 stores, but Results says 16 of the 23.

The other numbers agree: 14.2% to 9.8% is 4.4 points, minus the control's 0.9 points gives the net 3.5 points; the 0.6% and 0.9% labor-spend figures fit "within 1% of plan"; and the January start and 30 November integration date match.

items.output: ETA model v2 cuts mean absolute error from 11.2 to 8.9 minutes, a reduction of about 21%, in the five metro areas we evaluated (Austin, Denver, Columbus, Tampa, and Phoenix) on August data. The new model adds a live-traffic feature to the v1 inputs. It does not yet include a weather feature, and we have not checked how it performs in storms. Our analysis suggests that a substantial portion of new sign-ups drop off at the identity verification step. About 40% of users who start verification never complete it. This may be linked to the document upload requirement, although we have not isolated the cause.

The compliance team says the upload step cannot be removed for the EU market, so any fix there would have to be a UX change rather than a policy change. The design team believes a redesigned upload screen could recover a meaningful share of these users, but this is a hypothesis rather than a measured result.

We are planning to run a prototype test in the week of 8 February and will circulate results by the end of that month.
items.notes: Why it sounded off: it opened with thanks and "truly eye-opening", then announced "a high-level overview of the key takeaways" instead of giving them. It stacked hedges ("based on our analysis, it seems", "could potentially"), and it closed with a cheerful "feel free to reach out!". None of those lines carried a fact. The real content was solid and is all still here: the 40% figure, the unisolated cause, the compliance constraint, the unmeasured design hypothesis, and the February test. I kept the single hedge on each uncertain claim and the attributions to compliance and design.
